utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. There's one leftover from the past month, I would say -- no, perhaps even years which I'd like to deal with first before we continue to hear the final argument of the Defence. It is about admission of D1086. On the 30th of June of 2015, during the testimony of Bruno Franjic, the Chamber reserved Exhibit Number D1086 for a photograph shown to the witness but not yet uploaded into e-court. This can be found at transcript page 36500. The Defence only uploaded this photograph and sought its admission on the 5th of December, 2016, after having been reminded of this issue by the Registry. On the 7th of December, 2016, the Prosecution informed the Defence and the Chamber that it does not object to the photograph's admission. The Chamber recalls that the photograph was shown to a witness during the Defence case. While the evidentiary phase of the case is over, given the fact that there are no objections to the document's admission, in the specific circumstances of this document, the Chamber will exceptionally admit the document at this stage of the proceedings. And the Chamber instructs the Registry to assign D1086 to Rule 65 ter number 1D05459a and admits D1086 in evidence. Mr. Ivetic, if you're ready to continue your final argument, then proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you. Before I continue with our arguments, I owe two corrections of citations which we gave last week and which you raised questions about at the end of Friday. As to the combat casualties of the column and Mr. Butler's evidence and that of others, that is to be found at paragraphs 2738 through 2751 of our final trial brief, and not paragraph 2264 which I had erroneously read out in court. Likewise, in regards to genocide the second Mladic correspondence complaining of Arkan's activities in Sanski Most from September/October 1995, should be P03095, rather than D929 which I had read out and which Your Honours rightly noted which was a witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, of course, during the final argument we're not able to check every source, et cetera, but in few of the fact that the small number I did verify, there were quite a few mistakes, as there was a mistake as well for the Prosecution, would you please take care -- or perhaps check again, that your references are right, because now it's easy to correct them, but in a later stage to have communication with the parties after the final arguments have been closed is not something we're looking forward to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will resume our submissions as to genocide. Your Honours, it cannot be established that there was a pattern of crimes or a co-ordinated plan to commit genocide in the municipalities, as set out in the Defence final brief in greater detail; incidents occurred based on local circumstances and by different perpetrators. Violence was affected by the level of trust that existed in a local -- on a local level between the different communities. In Prijedor, memories of World War II were still fresh in the mind of most Bosnian Serb residents and the level of trust between the different ethnicities was limited; as example, we have D859 and D62. However, in other places, such as Srbac, the situation remained peaceful, despite ethnic Croat forces shelling Srbac on several occasions in 1992, and we had the evidence of Witness Milincic as to see that at transcript page 28350 through 28352. General Mladic made all efforts to sedate and quell any upsurge in violence or move towards conflict. This is evidenced, for instance, by the fact that he was an absolute proponent of the peaceful approach resolution as adopted in Srbac by Milincic and Mladic repeated this in front of 500 people in a meeting. We have that again from Witness Milincic at T28350 through 28352 and also in D783, paragraphs 15, 24, 25. The Prosecution claims that prominent members of the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat side were targeted, this is at paragraph 355 of their final brief. It is not logical in any war that individuals from the opposing party, such as commanders or prominent members stirring up fighting, are arrested. The intention of Mladic and the VRS was not to kill prominent members, it was merely to arrest enemy combatants as legitimate prisoners of war which is not a crime and which is based upon their threat to peace and security not their ethnic identity. The killings that occurred were unintended and certainly not ordered or planned by Mladic and, in fact, reporting to Mladic was not always available or talked of steps taken against perpetrators. The inclusion of non-Serbs into the ranks of the VRS, including Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croats including within Prijedor municipality, demonstrates that there was no discriminatory intent, let alone an intent to destroy non-Serbs in whole or in part within the mind of the accused. And as examples we have P7406, paragraph 2, we have the testimony of Witness Kelecevic at 37360 through 37364; D767; D768; D769, among others. As the Appeals Chamber in Tolimir confirmed, the selective targeting of a protected group's leadership may amount to genocide only if the leaders are selected because of the impact that their disappearance would have on the survival of the group as such that. That was in paragraph 265 of that judgement. No evidence in the instant case demonstrates that the legitimate detainees had significant impact on the physical survival of the Bosnian Muslims and Croats. In their closing arguments, the Prosecution claims that the Defence ignores the jurisprudence as to targeting of a leadership group; the Prosecution is misrepresenting the Defence position. We take no issue with the law. Rather, we are saying that in the particular instances that were cited, such as Prijedor, the factual circumstances do not demonstrate the type of targeting with the specific intent to destroy, as is required under the same jurisprudence cited by the Prosecution. The Prosecution has alleged that the departure of people from the municipalities substantiates a claim of forcible transfer and of genocide; however, when taken in its totality, the evidence demonstrates that people chose to leave the different municipalities for a variety of reasons - as Mr. Lukic has already mentioned last week - such reasons for departure, having no basis in the existence of any JCE or acts of the accused or the VRS. The Prosecution starts with the presupposition that persons left due to a JCE and due to acts of the VRS and thus sees a pattern because it has blinded itself to all other alternative interpretations. The evidence from municipalities does not show forcible removal at the hands of the VRS as its only conclusion. An allegation of forcible transfer is insufficiently evidenced on this basis. In addition, as we noted in the Prlic et. al trial judgement, to substantiate a claim the Prosecution -- such a claim, the Prosecution must show that the people of the municipalities left because of a criminal act by Mladic. That was in paragraph 55 of that judgement. More importantly, to substantiate the greater allegation of genocide, the Prosecution must prove there was a specific shared genocidal intent between the perpetrators of these acts and General Mladic. Only demonstrating that people left is not enough. Evidence needs to be presented that ties General Mladic specifically to the intent to destroy that specific segment of the population, and we would cite to the ICJ Bosnia versus Serbia and Montenegro judgement, paragraph 190; the Tolimir appeals judgement, paragraph 231; and the Stakic trial judgement, paragraphs 519 and 533. We submit this cannot be established. Many people left before Mladic was even appointed as Main Staff commander of the VRS, so how could he have had the intent to forcibly remove and destroy them? And where is the evidence of meetings where he would have agreed to commit these alleged crimes? How can such a grandiose, criminal plan be effectuated across so many municipalities absent any meetings or any written orders? It could not. That is why an acquittal is appropriate. Moreover, when combat takes place between two opposing forces, both forces have the obligation to remove people temporarily from possible harm. Additional Protocol I Article 58(a) and Article 49 of Convention IV. In the necessary circumstances this obligation was followed by the VRS. The fulfilment of an obligation required under international law cannot, in all practicality, then be used by the Prosecution to evidence a claim of genocide. If the VRS had not temporarily removed the civilians, people would have been left unprotected and risked being killed in combat. Your Honours, several Chambers from this Tribunal have examined the allegation of genocide in the municipalities. In each one, the defendant has been acquitted of this charge. For instance, the Stakic Appeals Chamber reaffirmed the Trial Chamber decision to acquit on this charge. They found there was insufficient evidence to support the proposition that the elected civilian leadership of the RS developed a genocidal campaign. Similarly, in relation to Prijedor, the OTP's main focus, the Brdjanin chamber specifically determined the absence of an escalation to genocide in the ARK after examining the killings at Koricanske Stijene and treatment of prisoners at Keraterm, Omarska, Trnopolje, and the situation in Prijedor, Kljuc, and Sanski Most. And even in the most closely related case to the one that is before Your Honours, the Karadzic case, that Trial Chamber found that after a holistic approach and reviewing statements in their context, it could not be established that there was an intent to destroy Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats in whole or in part in any municipality in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In this case, the Prosecution has not presented any new evidence that would result in a different conclusion. When considering the evidence in whole together with all the facts and circumstances in this case, it cannot be established that the intent to destroy the Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats is the only reasonable inference the Trial Chamber can make. Thus, this leads to only one possible conclusion: The accused should be acquitted of Count 1. Now, we may deal with some of the other municipalities later, but insofar as the Prosecution has shined their spot-light on Prijedor, I would like to spend some time focussing on this municipality and the evidence to demonstrate how the Prosecution's case fails to eliminate reasonable doubt because conclusions inconsistent with the Prosecution indictment can be reached under the available evidence. We have set forth substantial arguments as to Prijedor and Tomasica within our final brief at sections III(B) and (C). The Prosecution would like to use Prijedor as its model municipality for the charges relating to genocide in the municipalities; however, to do so, the Prosecution mis-argues the facts and misrepresents the same and also hopes that you will forget or ignore counter-conclusions which exist under the evidence, which is not appropriate. The existence of counter-conclusions under the evidence, acts under in dubio pro reo, to establish reasonable doubt and indicates that the Prosecution has not met the burden of proof. We highlight only some factors relevant to Prijedor. The Prosecution claims that the departure of civilians from Prijedor was part of a joint criminal enterprise to remove or destroy all non-Serbs, and in their final brief they say this started with the take-over of power by Serbs in Prijedor. Now, that's in Annex A of the final brief, in paragraphs 2 and 9 relating to Prijedor. And further, they say, it was started by efforts to disarm non-Serb villages in the Hambarine, Kozarac areas, including Brdo, also Annex A of the Prosecution's paragraph, paragraphs 15 through 17 dealing with Prijedor. They ignore that alternative conclusions are available from the evidence; namely, that lack of electricity, lack of consumer products, and shortages of other essential items meant that Prijedor was running on 10 to 15 per cent of its capacities and people were trying to survive with these shortages. The Prosecution's own exhibit, P4131, establishes this. So not just non-Serbs but Serbs as well were dealing with these shortages. Other documents and evidence also showed shortages of medicine, electricity, water, and food in Prijedor. P338, page 146; P3278, page 17; we had a Prosecution witness testified about this at T2097; and we had also P3847 [Realtime transcript read in error "P7847"], page 11; P7385, page 26. In such a situation, common sense and logic state that some persons will leave an area with these shortages to go somewhere elsewhere where they think it is better or where it actually is better. The evidence is that entire neighbourhoods and villages in Prijedor that were ethnically non-Serb in population stayed even throughout the war, which demonstrates a logical and reasonable conclusion that there was not an intent to destroy or remove non-Serbs. Further, although the Prosecution claims that non-Serb police commanders were removed after the take-over due to ethnicity, the evidence does not support that view. Prosecution witnesses confirmed, rather, that non-Serbs retained their jobs until the attack in Hambarine. We can find that at transcript 3506 through 3507 and also at P2585. After the attack at the check-point in Hambarine, many Bosnian Muslims and Croats simply stopped going to work; again, RM0206 told us about that in P2585. I ask you: How can General Mladic be responsible for the acts of these individuals to stop going to work? Further, there is evidence that police officers, both Bosnian Muslims and Croats, were offered the option of staying in their positions provided that they accept the state, Republika Srpska, and its laws. We see this from P3948, page 3. And this was true for Serbs too. Those who refused, independent of their ethnicity, were dismissed. And we can see that from the Prosecution witness T3394 through 3395, Merdzanic; and then we can also see that at D61, D62. Is this some criminal plan or a legitimate action to protect against sedition? Further, police officers from the Prijedor area of Bosnian Muslim or Croat region were given the opportunity to stay employed as members of the Kozarac police station. We see that from D1771 [Realtime transcript read in error "D1717"], page 58. Simply put, the evidence does not support the Prosecution; but rather, together with the common sense and logic, this evidence show there is was no JCE to commit genocide or otherwise. Everyone was trying to re-establish peace. And again, all of this takes place before General Mladic is even on the ground because he is still in Croatia. To be guilty of what the Prosecution charges, General Mladic must have had superhuman powers. Likewise, we also have heard evidence of a significant number of non-Serbs who were mobilized into and served in the VRS even after the events in Prijedor. Again, we have D767, D768, D769, the testimony of Witness Javoric at transcript page 31402 through 3 and the testimony of Witness Sipovac at 28143.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you earlier, some ten lines from where we are now, you referred to D1717. I don't know whether there's a transcription error or whether you misspoke, but could you please check what you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It should be D1771 and page 58 of the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again, the mobilisation and service of non-Serbs in the VRS demonstrates that the VRS and General Mladic did not intend any kind of genocide, destruction, or removal of non-Serbs, but rather was engaged in a legitimate defence of all loyal citizens of the Republika Srpska against armed enemies. D896 is a list of conscripts and shows that there were 381 ethnic Croats present, 108 ethnic Bosniaks, 78 Ukrainians, and also some soldiers from other nationalities in Prijedor -- in Prijedor's VRS units. Rodic explained how he compiled this document. Bosnian Croats and Muslims accounted for more than 10 per cent of the VRS in the Prijedor area throughout the war and some units had 20 to 30 per cent Bosnian Croat and Muslim members in their ranks. Sipovac testified as to that at 28145, and we see that also in D896, D767. Witness Rodic stated that more than 12 per cent of the personal engaged in the 6th and 2nd Battalions of the 43rd Motorised Brigade were all non-Serb ethnicities and that the Prijedor Garrison Command was resolved to equally protect all citizens in the territory of Prijedor municipality, regardless of their ethnicity, and it invited them to join the ranks of the VRS; D930 [Realtime transcript read in error "D390"], paragraph 23. Witness Javoric confirmed that units of the VRS which included Croats and Muslims were also engaged in breaking through the corridor, and that was at transcript page 31401. And Witness Sipovac stated at transcript page 28143: "The Ljubija Battalion, the 6th Motorised Battalion, was manned by people from a multi-ethnic area and the makeup included Serbs, Croats, and Muslims." If one wants to destroy someone, you don't invite them to join your army and give them weapons; rather, a contrary conclusion is available under this evidence. Are these non-Serb officers and soldiers of the VRS committing genocide against themselves? Against their families? That defies logic. The Prosecution case thus defies logic, and therefore, you must acquit. The Prosecution's misguided theory of the VRS's involvement in genocide is contrary to even Prosecution evidence. We have P2874, a 21 May 1992 order from the command of the 1st Krajina Corps of the VRS which covers the Prijedor area. In it, the intent is made clear that the VRS is the army not just of the Serb people but of all patriots, as well as of all citizens, who are ready to fight in its ranks for the just goals of the Serbian people, the defence of the territorial integrity of the republic, and peace in these areas. Most importantly, the order finishes by saying: "This army is fighting for truth, freedom, and the fatherland, for the survival of its own people, for peace and progress, and therefore its conduct, both towards its own people and towards the enemy, must be dignified, moral, and chivalrous." Does that sound like an illegal order to commit crimes? Or is it, as common sense would dictate, a proper and appropriate order under the circumstances? Now let's take a brief look at the circumstances, but before we do, you have to ask yourselves: How can the Prosecution meet its high burden to prove -- of proof, especially as to dolus specialus, of genocide if it cannot show actual orders emanating from the VRS top, from Mladic himself, to commit genocide in Prijedor? If their case is so strong, where are these order? All they can do is ask you to misconstrue ambiguities in statements or orders of other, not Mladic. Now as to the circumstances or context of Prijedor, that must be understood to understand why people would legitimately leave due to legitimate combat activities and why armed action against enemy forces in villages were legitimate. On 29 [Realtime transcript read in error "19"] April 1992, a coded cable arrived from the Bosnian Muslim police headquarters in Sarajevo and instructed Bosnian Muslims to attack the Serbs. We have that in evidence at D624 and D625.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I heard you saying on 29th of April; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours, 29 April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then the transcript has to be corrected. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This had been sent by the Bosnian Muslim MUP and the Bosnian Serb TO, Alija Delimustafic, Hasan Efendic, in Sarajevo to their brethren in Prijedor and elsewhere and in Prijedor due to a Muslim officer changing his duty shift, this was discovered by a Serb police officer who replaced him. Witness Mandzic talked about that at D826, paragraph 9. As a result, Serb politicians decided - with the assistance of the local police - P288; P7634, page 1; P3917, page 4, they decided to take over power of the Prijedor municipality and did so on 30 April 1992. We have that at D895, paragraph 21; D826, paragraph 9. It must again be stressed that all these actions were undertaken before General Mladic was commander of the Main Staff, so how can he held responsible for something he do not even control? Again, is he a superhuman being? Again, anything more than just the tip of the pyramid, and you must acquit. The reality of the Serb fear for attacks and the authenticity of this cable were confirmed by attacks initiated against the JNA on the 2nd and 3rd of May, 1992, at Dobrovoljacka Street in Sarajevo when the JNA started withdrawing from the Sarajevo barracks, they were attacked by the ABiH. We have that from Prosecution Witness Doyle at transcript page 1599; Exhibit P91, paragraph 94; Exhibit D711, paragraph 2; Exhibit D622, paragraphs 19 through 21; Exhibit D645, paragraph 7, and others. These attacks an actions were in perfect accord with the cable, as it responded to the call for attacks within that cable. And again, look at the cable, D625. We cannot stress enough that the Serb take-over of power in Prijedor, which was accomplished without a shot being fired and which achieved -- and which was achieve any involvement of General Mladic, resulted in that things were calm and peaceful up until 22nd May, 1992, P3617, page 7; Witness Dragojevic transcript 35605 to 35606. The evidence shows several initiatives were taken by the Serbs to meet with the Bosnian Muslims and Croats in order to prevent armed conflict. P4160, page 1 through 2; Witness Vujic, transcript page 35053. Things not erupt further in Prijedor until distinction hostile events undertaken by armed Muslim paramilitary forces which, again, were taken akin to the actions that were called for in the coded cable we just talked about. On 22 May 1992, six VRS soldiers, two of whom were ethnic Bosnian Croats, were stopped and attacked in Hambarine at a Bosnian Muslim check-point for no reason. We see that from D912; P482; P2900, page 15; D834, pages 2 through 9; D895, paragraphs 22 through 23, among others. Several VRS soldiers were killed or wounded including the non-Serbs, D912; P3987, paragraphs 2 and 10; P482, page 1; D863, paragraph 9, among others. A few days later, on 24 May 1992, Bosnian Muslim forces attacked again, this time on a VRS military column near Kozarac, D895, paragraph 25; Witness Javoric, transcript page 31491; P4160; P3555. As is to be expected, these acts staged by Bosnian Muslims created chaos and legitimate fears for both the Serb and non-Serb population. It goes without saying General Mladic did not control the Muslim forces that started this chaos. Again it must be stressed that the Prosecution points to the efforts to disarm the non-Serb paramilitaries in these villages and implies that is an essential part of the alleged JCE. Now, the use to support -- as support for this proposition, an ultimatum issued by Major Zeljaja on 16 May 1992, and this is paragraph 15 of the Prosecution brief as to Prijedor. We have various evidence indicating that these forces of the Bosnian Muslims from these villages were significantly armed, for instance, P2894, P4061, D390, P7299, among others. But what is instructive is what are the words that Zeljaja used for this ultimatum? And I want to read from the evidence a key Prosecution witness who testified at transcript page 3461 through 5 about these words and he remembered them as being: "Unless you surrender 7.000 weapons and unless the Serbian flag is flying over Kozarac and the Serb police have control, I'll raze Kozarac to the ground." And he said at the end: "When you return those weapons, then we can go on talking." Now, he didn't say: I will raze the area if you surrender weapons. No, he says: If you surrender weapons, we can negotiate. Well, what is this? Common sense dictates that it can also be understood as a legitimate example of a military doctrine known as defended city, where a locality refuses to open and vacate military forces, it is a defended city and is a legitimate target so long as it mounts a defence. If it surrenders armaments, then it cannot be attacked. The Prosecution likes to play word games and in paragraph 18 as to Prijedor they characterise these armed Muslims as "poorly armed" and as members of the "population." But in law, presence of armed combatants or civilians directly engaging in combat and mixing with combatants renders even a civilian area as a defended city as a legitimate target. Now, another Prosecution witness, protected witness so I won't mention the name, testified in P3121 and his recollection of the words of VRS Commander Zeljaja are even more informative, and again, this is still the 16 May 1992 ultimatum. He recalls: "There can be no negotiations. There's no more Yugoslav People's Army. From today on we are Serbian Army and all members of the Territorial Defence and the reserve police force are hereby requested to turn in all of their weapons. All citizens of Bosniak ethnicity shall declare their loyalty to the Serbian Republic and shall respond to the mobilisation into the Serbian Army." Now, this is similar to what we referred to earlier. In the midst of this confrontation, with shots already fired, the VRS is not telling non-Serbs to leave Prijedor; to the contrary, it is imploring them to disarm, stay, and become loyal citizens of the Serbian Republic. And all the more, he is asking them to join him in the VRS army. Now this cannot be warped by the Prosecution into a call to commit genocide against these same persons. What is further, the Prosecution ignores the greater context of events; namely, prior to this point the BiH has ordered the JNA out of Bosnia and the JNA has agreed to do so weeks prior, D1661, P4412, D829. And in the greater context, the UN Security Council - in fact, just one day prior on 15 May 1992 - has stated that the Yugoslav Army must depart, so this part of the ultimatum saying there is no more JNA comes directly from that. We have P2052 talking about the Security Council Resolution. And now I'd like to look at a slide. Also in the same resolution, again a day before this ultimatum is issued, UN Security Council Resolution 752 - and we have various documents talking about that in evidence, P2815, P1999, the Donia report at page 85 - this resolution has five demands of the Security Council. Number five is instructive for us here and it says: "All irregular forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina be disbanded and disarmed." So in light of this context, the ultimatum of Zeljaja one day later takes on a new meaning. Unless the Prosecution wants to label this UN Security Council Resolution as their smoking gun, their order to commit genocide - and if they do then the UN Secretary-General and not General Mladic should be in the dock - but under this evidence and these facts, it is reasonable to conclude that the calls to disarm by Zeljaja were an attempt, perhaps poorly effectuated, but an attempt to comply with UN resolutions. On 30 May 1992 there was an attack on the town of Prijedor by approximately 80 armed Bosnian Muslim men; that's evidenced at P2876, page 2. On this day, early in the morning, this Bosnian Muslim and Croat armed group attacked the town of Prijedor causing chaos and surprising everyone. At this point, the VRS was not yet present in this place. We have the testimony of Witness Jesic at 29928 [Realtime transcript read in error "29918"] of the transcript, P4068; D1041, paragraph 5; D826, paragraph 21. It is clear from the evidence that the Bosnian Muslim and Croat forces had a structured plan. They were well trained and beforehand had multiple groups which were tasked to attack versus key places. Their aim was to take control over vital buildings in Prijedor, such as the MUP and the municipal building, D930, Witness Rodic; D826, Witness Mandzic, and they succeeded at first. As they made it to the centre of town, they tried to set the hotel on fire and were engaged in fighting in front of the municipal building, P2876, D930, and Witness Mandic talked about that. While the Prosecution claims that the old town, also known as Stari Grad, was attacked by the Serbs as part of a JCE, that's at paragraph 21 of their Annex A section as to Prijedor, the total picture shows evidence that Bosnian Muslims and Croats after the attack on the town of Prijedor withdrew their forces to Stari Grad and engaged in attacks from that part of the town, D859, paragraph 13; Witness Vujic, transcript page 34500. During all the attacks at least 17 members of the Serb police were killed and a large number was seriously or lightly wounded, D930, paragraph 11. Even innocent individuals such as Goran Dragojevic, an ambulance driver; and Witness Jesic were fired upon by the Bosnian Muslim and Croat forces and taken hostage and used as human shields, D1052, page 2; D1049, paragraph 7; Witness Jesic, transcript page 29919. Now, is General Mladic the one ordering these Muslims and Croats to attack Prijedor? Is he responsible for acts of the enemy? No. But these acts had a serious effect on Prijedor and sparked fears. Let's not forget that ethnic Croats and ethnic Muslims from some of these same villages in Prijedor during World War II attempted a genocide against Serbs. Recall that much evidence spoke of severe losses borne by Serb households in Prijedor from the world war. These memories, coupled with the successive armed hostile acts of Hambarine, Kozarac, and the attack on Prijedor - all three involving Bosnian Muslim and Croat armed paramilitary units - well, the effect was that people got scared and they overreacted, not due to any plan from Ratko Mladic, but rather, from genuine home-grown fear of the local population and local leaders that was triggered by these hostile acts of armed non-Serbs. And so detention centres were set up and actions were under taken to arrest non-Serb males suspected of being part of the attacks and they were investigated and triaged and were to be released when it became clear they were not involved in attacks, P4160, page 4; P2900, page 30; P480, page 76. These centres - Omarska and Keraterm - were not set up by the VRS. They were set up and controlled by the local Crisis Staff and the MUP civilian police, D1041 paragraph 8; P480, pages 20 and 21; P4160, pages 3 through 4; P2900, page 11 and 30, among other evidence. The army was not involved. Contrary to the Prosecution's ill-devised implication that the army had a role in these centres. At paragraph 33 of their final brief as to Prijedor, the Prosecution has even conceded that Keraterm and Omarska were run by the SJB Prijedor, the civilian police. For both centres, the VRS was requested to take over the management an operation, but the VRS refused and therefore never became involved in it, D1111; D852, paragraph 43. In Keraterm, the VRS was only located outside the parameter in an out-building of the Keraterm complex but never went inside the centre itself; Witness Rodic talked about that at transcript page 33067. At Omarska, the VRS only performed guard duty again on the outer parameter outside the compound; Witness Rodic talked about that at transcript page 33110. General Mladic cannot be held responsible for actions of civilian authorities. As for Trnopolje, this was a refugee centre, established again by the Prijedor Crisis Staff and managed by the TO and local police. We have Witness Kelecevic at transcript page 37263; P02900, page 2. Despite the Prosecution's claims to the contrary, reasonable doubt exists as to whether and when Kuruzovic was a member of the army. The Prosecution, in fact, now presents two differing accounts of the date that Kuruzovic allegedly was incorporated into the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, your reference to a P document, can you repeat the number please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Gladly. It should be P02900, page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: 2900. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now the Prosecution presents two differing accounts of the date that Kuruzovic allegedly was incorporated into the VRS. Remember, if they present contradictory evidence, reasonable doubt exists and you must acquit. The evidence is clear that Kuruzovic existed as a part of the separate municipal TO apart from the VRS. The evidence is clear that the Serbian Prijedor Territorial Defence continued to exist until at least 16 September 1992, D2179. And, Your Honours, I see we're at the time for the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are, Mr. Ivetic. We'll take that break now and we'll resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Before I resume, my colleagues have found a couple of corrections that I can put on record. Temporary transcript page 9, line 4, what is recorded as P7847 should be P3847. Temporary transcript page 15, line 13, instead of D390 it should be D930. And temporary transcript page 18, line 2, instead of transcript page 29918, it should be 29928 for Witness Jesic. And now I'll resume. Trnopolje was certainly not a camp or a detention centre as alleged by the Prosecution in paragraph 41 of their final brief as to Prijedor. On the contrary, it was an open reception centre providing safety for refugees fleeing from the conflict and fleeing from Muslim extremists, P3528 [sic], P5149, among other documents and witnesses spoke of that. In addition, organisations such as the International Red Cross, Merhamet, and Doctors Without Borders and Pharmacists Without Borders regularly visited the centre, P5149. This undermines the Prosecution argument that the Serbs had a JCE to commit genocide and destroy these peoples; reasonable doubt exists and you must acquit. In the centres, the police operative officers were the ones who carried out processing and investigative tasks. Only one VRS member was involved in the alleged mixed interrogation teams and that was Lieutenant-Colonel Majstorovic. The participation of Majstorovic in these interrogations has to be observed in light of P2895, where Majstorovic is mentioned as being responsible for investigators. Paragraph 4 of this document states that they cannot only be absent with the permission of Simo Drljaca and paragraphs 11 and 15 show they are only allowed to report to Simo Drljaca and not the VRS. General Kelecevic even confirmed that he had no idea Majstorovic was in Omarska until after the war. Given this evidence, this clearly demonstrates that Majstorovic acted of his own accord and under the instructions of Drljaca and was not even allowed to follow instructions of the VRS; thus, General Mladic cannot be held responsible. Now did this atmosphere of fear and chaos in Prijedor contribute to people leaving? It probably did, all peoples. Did regrettable excesses and even deaths in the way of collateral damage or even killings happen in combat, clearing the terrain, or in these civilian-run detention facilities? Probably, but it was neither intended, planned, ordered, nor known by General Mladic. We are not here today judging Simo Drljaca of the Prijedor MUP, nor are we judging other local leaders. General Mladic can only answer for his conduct and allegations of his crimes, not the conduct and crimes of others beyond his effective control. One must look at the reporting that comes to General Mladic about the alleged crimes in Keraterm and Omarska. He does not get much information as these are police centres. There is evidence, for instance, that for the infamous so-called Room 3 massacre, P161, a report sent to the Main Staff, talks of a mass escape that was attempted and thwarted with 50 prisoners killed in the process. Now, this report does not raise any illegality in the deaths so as to put General Mladic on notice, nor create a nexus between him and the actions of the police that control Keraterm. Logically, and reasonably, and in accord with in dubio pro reo, we can conclude a benign and non-criminal conclusion from this report. Likewise, P248, dated the very next day, talks of a new attempt to escape, which was thwarted in time. There is it no talk of deaths. Now, General Mladic does not have a duty to investigate if the reporting is accurate based on what is reported in these two reports; as such, there is no nexus between these incidents - irrespective of whether a crime or not - and General Mladic. As to Omarska, the evidence is clear that no reporting came to Mladic. SJB Chief Drljaca was in charge of Omarska, P4136, just as he was in charge of Keraterm. In evidence we have P2895 and at pages 2 to 3 it states that security services at the collection centre shall be provided by the Omarska police station. This document signed by Drljaca also states: "I most strictly prohibit giving any information whatsoever concerning the functioning of this collection centre. All official documents shall be kept at the collection centre and may be taken out or destroyed only with the permission of the chief of the Prijedor public security station. This shall be the responsibility of the security staff." The implementation of this order was supposed to be supervised by Police Chief Dusan Jankovic. If can I have the next slide, next, there. I may have talked about this earlier, but in the Prosecution's brief they imply that General Mladic issued an order for these MUP camps to be cleaned up before a visit of the ICRC and media. And what we have on the screen is P2879 which the Prosecution uses as support for this. But if you look at the recipients, is it sent to Keraterm or Omarska? No, it isn't. It is in relation to only Omarska and Keraterm? No, it didn't. As is plainly evident from the plain text of this order, Mladic is telling the subordinate commander to prepare for a visit to several places including, Manjaca, which is a VRS facility, and asks that the subordinate commander contact the MUP in relation to other facilities on the Territorial Defence. If Mladic were directing the actions at Omarska and Keraterm, he would send this order directly to those facilities an order them to do so; he cannot. Now, let's go to the next slide. And if we look at another document, P201, and this is Talic's order after receiving the previous order from Mladic. And, again, he can send it straight to Manjaca because Manjaca is a VRS facility, but he has no authority as to Omarska, Keraterm, or Trnopolje, and that is why he has to send this order to the civilian police station in Prijedor. You cannot mistake these two documents as the VRS having any role in Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje. It is just by nature of the fact that the same visit also included Manjaca. Now, we also have other evidence that the media and ICRC required civilian approval for this trip. P205 is a memorialisation of that same on film and P200 as well. Now, let's get back to the knowledge of General Mladic as to all those actions in the various villages to disarm and clear the terrain in Prijedor. And as a starting point, the Prosecution attempts to place a nefarious and illegal connotation to a legitimate military term and tactic known as clearing up or cleansing the terrain, "ciscenje," and sometimes it's referred to as mopping up. Their own insider witness who is protected, so again I will not say the name, by RM097 at our trial differentiated between legitimate military "ciscenje," as taught in the JNA, from any forceable removal of civilians as claimed by the OTP. This was at transcript pages 17845 to 17847. There can be no doubt that "ciscenje," as used in the military sense, does not include the forceable removals that this witness claimed to have seen. And I think we have one more slide. But now let's look at P2440 from the 6th Partisan Brigade signed by Colonel Basara, and the same protected Prosecution witness we talked about confirmed that this appeared to be the same operation he was talking about as to Prijedor villages where he saw this activity that was different from "ciscenje." And in this order, first we see in item 2 of the same: "Destroy armed enemy groups with sudden fire, and take unarmed persons fit for combat to the Milin Birt area, from where they will be transported onward. Leave women, children, and old men in their homes." And then on page 3 of this document which is the second excerpt on the screen, we have a supplement to this order that says: "Do not set fire to houses. Looting is forbidden. Leave the population alone if they are peaceful. Only lock up the extremists. Liquidate armed groups." Thus, Your Honours, based upon these order, anyone persons seen by any witness claimed to be VRS who are forcing civilians from their homes in this operation are acting contrary to the express orders of the VRS, and therefore cannot be a basis for the liability of General Mladic unless he has knowledge of those actions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you provide with us the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm. We could get that perhaps by the next break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the body of evidence as to the reporting on these activities, we see no such information or knowledge of crimes being reported to Mladic. The Prosecution highlights several reports in paragraph 19 of its final brief as to Prijedor, but if one actually reads the documents cited by the Prosecution in this paragraph, all the other evidence also cited, we see that none of these give notice of crimes against civilians, but rather talk of legitimate military actions against Green Berets and members of paramilitary formations. And, Your Honour, as to your question, P2440 is dated the 18th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again, if General Mladic is getting this kind of reporting, even if perhaps not entirely accurate, he cannot be blamed for the actions. Lastly on this topic, the Prosecution attempts to raise a lot of smoke and mirrors by referring to a report by Talic to the Main Staff, P3697, and this is at paragraph 25 of their final brief. But Talic is reporting that all activities are proceeding in accord with Directive 1. Now, the Prosecution would like to imply that this means that it's talking about crimes, but if we recall Directive 1 and if we think about how Mladic - familiar with Directive 1 - would understand things are proceeding in accord with Directive 1, P474 was Directive 1, and we saw it earlier last week and it talked about treating -- about how to treat the civilian population that was not engaged in war properly and treating POWs in accord with law. So if Talic is reporting that everything is proceeding in accord with Directive 1, there can be no notice of any criminal activity. Now remarkably in the final brief the Prosecution spend a lot of time talking about and intending to prove VRS involvement in the crimes at Koricanske Stijene, that is paragraphs 46 and 47 of their brief. I'm shocked again that the Prosecution resorts to raising an unscheduled incident that has been crossed out because this was dropped from the indictment as 13.6, and thus it is wholly improper to try to revive that charge at the final brief stage. I have already talked about that last week and again would stress that Your Honours should enter an acquittal if the Prosecution insists in seeking a conviction for Koricanske Stijene. Now, even apart from the procedural and legal aspect, all the evidence demonstrates that it was not the VRS but rather the police intervention squad of the MUP - and again Simo Drljaca - who were involved in Koricanske Stijene. The -- all the orders received as to Koricanske Stijene came from the MUP, P2432. Rather, the VRS acted the opposite of the police. As soon as the VRS commander was involved of this incident, Peulic, he sent soldiers to the spot. He didn't send them to cover up the crime or kill anyone, but to see what could be done to save any victims. And survivors were taken by the VRS to the hospital, transcript page 2075; P154, paragraph 34; D887, paragraph 19. And, again, we have evidence that Drljaca and the MUP undertook to cover up these crimes. After Koricanske Stijene, there was a meeting with police officials at the Prijedor SUP to discuss what happened; the VRS was not present, P2432. And as soon as Drljaca noticed there would be an investigation into the incident, he tried to cover it up and responded to the Banja Luka security service that it was not possible to conduct an investigation as the men were sent to Han Pijesak. P2342 indicates that the MUP police destroyed all documentation about Koricanske Stijene and other crimes of the intervention platoon, that's at pages 52 through 53 and 85. These methods cannot be attributed in any way to the VRS and General Mladic. The allegation of the Prosecution in paragraph 47 of their final brief that some men were deployed to Han Pijesak as VRS members after they did the Koricanske Stijene crimes is not true. The intervention platoon were sent as members of a SUP mission to Han Pijesak, RM097; P2432, page 86. Therefore, all the mentioned evidence can only lead to one possible conclusion: General Mladic is not responsible for the unscheduled incident in Koricanske Stijene. Now I want to move a related area, the Tomasica evidence, which was part of the re-opening of the Prosecution case. The Prosecution presented a total of six purported experts as to Tomasica, yet this evidence was rather unspectacular and thin such that no findings of criminal liability could be supported by the same. This was acknowledged by the Trial Chamber in relation to several of the witnesses, including forensic ballistics expert Franjic and forensic DNA expert Karahasanovic. The Prosecution also presented a handful of fact witnesses. None of these could establish beyond requisite doubt any involvement of VRS personnel participating in the burials at Tomasica under orders from Ratko Mladic. Yet the Prosecution dramatically at paragraph 48 of the Prijedor section of their final brief states: "The role of the VRS and other authorities in using mass graves to conceal crimes in Prijedor is encapsulated by the Tomasica mass grave and related sites." And claims bodies were disposed in the grave by VRS soldiers. But the Prosecution evidence does not establish that the only reasonable conclusion available is that the VRS was involved in the burials. Rather, the evidence raises the more logical conclusion that it was civilian MUP that performed this task. The main Prosecution witness stated that he received orders from Radisa Ljesnjak and that no VRS member was seen on the site of the grave; that's at transcript page 36210 to 36211. The man who was implicated, Radisa Ljesnjak, was never a member of the VRS according to other evidence, D1081, D1359. Defence evidence points to him being a member of the MUP, D1081; and Prosecution evidence indicated he might be a member of the Crisis Staff, P7311, paragraph 2. The Prosecution has not presented any evidence to indicate that Ljesnjak was a member of the VRS. The Prosecution's own evidence further points that all individuals involved in the burials, such as the bulldozer operator and people accompanying the truck, wore civilian clothes. I refer you to the evidence of -- transcript page 36189, 36211. The only persons in uniform both wearing camouflage JNA uniforms were Ljesnjak and Simo Drljaca of the SJB Prijedor, both of whom were present at the burials, P7311, paragraph 8. Now, in evidence it is clear that - especially in Prijedor - police wore similar if not identical uniforms to the army and the average person can be mistaken as the same. Let's look at some of the Prosecution evidence in living colour on the next slide. Here we see stills from versus Prosecution videos of persons in Prijedor. On the top left, we see Mr. Drljaca, who we know to be the SJB police chief, wearing a military uniform. The Prosecution's own witness, Vulliamy further --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you should slow down. I think the court reporter has some problems to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I apologise. The Prosecution's own witness Edward Vulliamy further identified those in the various videos, such that in the middle we have one of the Omarska guards in military camouflage uniform and across the top we have the -- again, Mr. Drljaca in uniform. Then across the bottom we have Mr. Stakic in camouflage uniform. And most instructive is the last picture where we see Mr. Stakic, Mr. Kovacevic, Mr. Drljaca, and Colonel Arsic with everyone except Kovacevic wearing the same military-style uniforms and Kovacevic is wearing a US military T-shirt. So this shows that the MUP, civilian organs, and the VRS in Prijedor all wore military camouflage uniforms. Given that there is this overlap of persons in uniform -- that is, of course, P3278, P205, and P212. Given that there is this overlap of persons in uniform in Prijedor, identifications based solely on uniforms, whether in regard to Tomasica or another aspect of Prijedor, like the Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje camps, must be taken suspect and the conclusion remains possible that MUP personnel are being misidentified and mistaken for VRS soldiers. As to Tomasica, one Prosecution witness talks of military police who allegedly assisted in the transcript of bodies to Tomasica from Keraterm; his statement is P7314 and this is at paragraphs 16 to 18. There is a slight problem with his testimony, however. Among the "military policemen" that he sees in uniform and driving the "military police" civilian car in front of him are, in fact, known MUP members. He identifies by name Sikirica, the Keraterm commander as we know him; and Dosen, whom we know to be one of the shift commanders; and he includes them as being dressed with white belts and thus part of the military police. Again, the Prosecution has already conceded Keraterm was run by the MUP, specifically SJB Prijedor. P7313 indicates that MUP guards at Keraterm wore military uniforms. Now, the Prosecution witness in question can be forgiven for misidentifying MUP at Keraterm as VRS military police, but the Prosecution cannot. They prosecuted and convicted both Dosen and Sikirica as police personnel before this very same Tribunal. They cannot feign ignorance. They cite to Sikirica's conviction in footnote 349 of their final brief. The minute they tender a statement that affirmatively claims that VRS were involved and that Sikirica and Dosen were two of those VRS involved, they have an affirmative obligation and duty to tell this court: Your Honours, we note pursuant to our duty of candor that both Dosen and Sikirica are SJB MUP and not VRS. Instead of this, the Prosecution dares to present this faulty statement as affirmative proof of VRS involvement, as some of the primary proof. During closing they also mentioned talk of other witnesses who saw persons in military uniforms at the burials. First, this is inconsistent with the other evidence that everyone was in civilian clothes; that is reasonable doubt. Second, that ignores the fact which we have now talked about that even police and civilian personnel wore uniforms; this is reasonable doubt. Likewise, persons mobilised for work duty, such as drivers, also were forced to wear a uniform, as the Prosecution's other evidence demonstrates; this, too, is reasonable doubt. Now let's look at how else the Tomasica burials are linked by the Prosecution to Ratko Mladic and the VRS. The Prosecution claims that machinery of the VRS was used, but the evidence is that VRS equipment was in Gradacac, in Modrica municipality, not Prijedor, 140 kilometres away at this time. Witness Vujic talked about that. Transcript page 41507. Your Honours may recall that the Prosecution attempted to present expert evidence by way of a report, P7441, prepared by forensic officers of the BiH investigating authorities, but they brought only one of three experts who signed the report, Witness Karahasanovic. After cross-examination and the witness disavowing her ability to discuss the expertise of the two remaining parts of the report, you - Judges Orie, Fluegge, Moloto - affirmatively ruled that you will not rely on the dactyloscopy part or chemical part of the report co-authored by Karahasanovic unless the other experts were called to testified. That's at transcript page 36555, 36567. But those witnesses were not brought, and thus the relevant parts of P7441 must be concluded from consideration as evidence. This includes the purported identification of JNA or VRS-style gas masks unearthed at Tomasica. Thus, it is shocking that although the Prosecution did not bring the experts in question to be crossed on the identification of the gas mask, they still want to rely on the same to prove the guilt of Ratko Mladic. And this is even after Your Honours have twice says you will not rely upon that part of the investigative report. They cite to this evidence you have excluded in footnote 304 of paragraph 50 of their Prijedor final brief. Now, because I want to leave no doubt - and this shows how desperate the Prosecution is - the identification of the gas mask was called into question in the cross of Karahasanovic, who again could not answer because her absent colleague did that part of the report. May we have the next slide. But, Your Honour, they say a picture is worth a thousand words, and so let's look together at what evidence shows us to be both the civilian and the military gas mask in question. And this is in evidence as D1090, the last page of that document is what we're looking at now on the screen. Now are they telling us that without an expert you are allowed to guess and conclude that the mask in question ask a VRS and army model, as opposed to the nearly identical civilian model? That for that a mask that has been buried for decades? Now, I won't even dwell on how the Bosnian MUP witnesses couldn't get their story straight as to who opened the evidence bags, who carried the evidence bags. Both Franjic and Karahasanovic pointed the finger elsewhere. Now, if you follow the law, if you adhere to in dubio pro reo and the burden of proof, no link can be concluded as to Tomasica under this evidence for my client, Ratko Mladic, and you must acquit. Now let's look at another Prosecution tactic as to Tomasica. In paragraph 52 of their final trial brief as to Prijedor, they make the claim that: "Evidence from autopsies of persons most recently exhumed is consistent with execution-style killings." And they cite to Dr. John Clark and they go on to focus on the number of injuries to the head as indicative of an execution. But, Your Honours, Dr. Clark was too smart to go beyond what the forensic science indicated and expressly disavowed this Prosecution position under oath. Rather than confirm that an execution was the cause of death, Dr. Clark admitted that he was not able to exclude the fact that people were killed in combat, transcript page 36651. And, in fact, Dr. Clark expressly deadlined to conclude based on the high frequency of head wounds that the deceased died as part of an execution, transcript page 36681 through 4. So why isn't the Prosecution honest and truthful about the evidence? Why does it want to put words in Clark's mouth that he did not agree to? Apart from Prosecution counsel, Ewa Tabeau also wanted so desperately to prove executions that she put words in Dr. Clark's mouth that he did not utter. Tabeau claimed the deceased were subjected to shooting from machine-guns or sometimes handguns, indicative of being machine-gunned down, P7449, page 23. Tabeau initially claimed that this was based on Dr. Clark's findings and that he supported her conclusion that these people had been victims of execution, transcript page 36807, 36808, 36830, 36831. However, after being confronted with the fact that even Dr. Clark's, on whose report she relied, did not use the term "machine-guns," Tabeau was forced to admit that while Clark used the term "high-velocity rifle," she mistakenly read that as "machine-gun" instead of the same and based on her erroneous conclusion. Thus, we have the Prosecution and Ewa Tabeau, so emotionally desperate to convince Your Honours to convict my client that they would misstate the evidence. Only an acquittal can remedy such a flagrant disrespect for justice and due process on the part of the Prosecution and Dr. Tabeau. I will only remind you that Dr. Stankovic clarified for us that in combat, the most often targeted and struck parts of the body are the head and the chest. Lastly, as to Tomasica, the Prosecution in paragraph 57 of their brief as to Prijedor misrepresent again a reference from what they claim to be the notebook of Ratko Mladic as to the knowledge of Simo Drljaca's cover-up in Tomasica. Assuming and taking the Prosecution at its word that this is Mladic's notebook, their evidence at best establishes a totally different conclusion. Given that this document is purported to be the notebook of the accused, it is thus illustrative to take this as evidence of no orders being issued by the accused to assist in burials or reburials or attempts to hide events in Tomasica. To the contrary, this document records the response of the accused to have been and is recorded as my position: They killed them so they should get rid of them and an investigation must be launched in connection with this case and the information retained well, to prevent it getting into the hands of unauthorised people. Thus, under this evidence, it is clear that the VRS and accused are hearing for the first time in 1993 about Tomasica, and the accused did not approve of the Tomasica burials nor reburials and did not authorise his subordinates to assist in the same but ordered that an appropriate investigation be launched into the events an actions of the MUP surrounding Tomasica and that the results of the investigation be safe-guarded for the appropriate, authorised organs to deal with. Under this set of facts, any individual VRS soldiers who may have participated in any aspect of Tomasica alongside the MUP would have done so without authorisation, for personal, individual reasons, and not under any orders from VRS commanders. In fact, they would be acting directly contrary to the only orders alleged to be issued by the accused, Ratko Mladic, according to the Prosecution's own evidence. Thus, no criminal responsibility could attach to the accused from the same. By the way, we heard a lot the other week, last week, from the Prosecution during their closing arguments that General Mladic and Mr. Drljaca were somehow close. This is a new tale that we hear for the first time in closing. Where is the evidence of such a relationship? Why is the evidence as to Prijedor full of references to Drljaca and no sign of Mladic with him? If anything, the Tomasica situation we have just been discussing demonstrates that General Mladic was neither close to Drljaca nor a fan of his. The Tomasica entry from the alleged notebook of the accused, which the Prosecution wants us to believe to be authentic, demonstrates bitterness and animosity of Mladic towards Drljaca. Further, it demonstrates that Drljaca hid Tomasica from Mladic. Under such evidence, the Prosecution's claim that Mladic and Drljaca were best buddies is unsubstantial. Remember, if they are trying to push more than just the tip of the pyramid of the burden of proof, that means reasonable doubt and you must acquit. Moving to the Prosecution's case as to overarching JCE, and I think we have a second slideshow for that. The Prosecution has failed to meet its burden of proof and thus no configuration can enter for General Mladic for the following reasons. Under the 1974 SFRY Constitution, Bosnia-Herzegovina functioned as a tripartite governing system comprising the three ethnic groups, with a number of mechanisms employed to safe-guard equality between the groups. Witnesses Dodik and Kecmanovic testified as to that at transcript page 42212 and 23807. The Bosnian Muslim and Croat parties violated this constitution to seek independence, while the Bosnian Serbs worked in good faith toward a peaceful solution, believing "it was better to negotiate for years than wage war for a few days," Witness Barasin, transcript page 28773. But the SDA began preparing for war by stockpiling weapons and arming themselves; D619, D614, D790 - among other evidence - demonstrates that. The effect of seeing Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats forming armed groups filled the Serbs with fear and panic, D675. The atmosphere of insecurity and fear was heightened when Muslim paramilitary groups began to mount attacks, D1690, page 8; D789, paragraph 36, including on Serb villages such as in Vecici, D1030. The atmosphere began to worsen with growing tensions described as "catastrophic," "absolute lawlessness," and "with chaos and terror against the members of the JNA." D414, page 1. It was during this time on 12 May 1992 that the accused was appointed VRS Main Staff commander. General Mladic was tasked with creating an army from a range of disparate group, including municipal-backed military groups, former Territorial Defence units, civilian conscripts, reserve officers, and volunteers, all with varying degrees of combat experience and skill. Integrating these distinct and structurally separate groups was a long and protracted process; witness Kovac testified about that, transcript page 41356 and 7. The accused is alleged to have contributed to the overarching JCE through his skilled and effective use of command and control as VRS Main Staff commander. Yet, during these initial stages, General Mladic's command and control was compromised by a number of factors. The Prosecution in their closing arguments alleged that the JNA 2nd Military District was a "well-functioning military that was part of the JCE in Bosnia," transcript page 44389. And they allege that Mladic took over this well-functioning military when appointed VRS Main Staff commander. Yet, what the Prosecution fails to mention is in its inception, the VRS Main Staff comprised only 12 officers, five of whom were generals. Both military experts of the Prosecution told us that, Butler at 16630 of the transcript and Dannatt at 19165 of the transcript. The VRS Main Staff was also positioned at the reserve command post of the 1st Army from Belgrade; Mr. Theunens discussed that at transcript page 20513. While the ABiH in Sarajevo on the other hand, inherited the buildings of the former JNA 4th Corps Command, D608, paragraph 21, which was a much better-equipped command position. Yet, the Prosecution would have you believe Ratko Mladic and his 12 men were the league of superheros to take on the ABiH and the whole world. The lack of professionally trained soldiers, officers, and junior officers created a lack of stabilisation for the entire army, Prosecution Witness Milovanovic, transcript page 17110, P4381. This was discussed extensively in the Defence final trial brief at paragraphs 651 to 676. Some examples include: Milorad Sehovac, a brigade commander in the SRK, who complained that his brigade was meant to be staffed with 82 officers but he only had three, including himself, D559, paragraph 31. How is it reasonable to assume that three professionally trained officers could exercise complete command and control over approximately 1.172 conscripts? D566, page 5. Similarly, on 5 March 1993, Colonel Balic of the 1st Birac Brigade reported a serious shortage of active-duty officers at the level of platoons, companies, and battalions, P5241, page 2. Another major factor that compromised the general's ability to exercise effective command and control over VRS forces was the failure of the civilian leadership to declare a state of war. This created, as General Sokanovic testified, many problems. A state of war had not been declared so that the army operated and worked under peacetime rules, even though it was in war already. That made command very difficult but also the other activities and responsibilities of the commands. That's what General Sokanovic told us at transcript page 35679, we also have that in P2201, paragraphs 4 through 9 and 11 [sic]. VRS soldiers took advantage of this by abandoning their positions, P5241, and generally ignoring orders to remain and fight, D1661. While the Prosecution would have you believe that the accused had absolute authority to run the war - that's what they said in their closing, transcript page 44332 to 44336 - the material facts show a radically different story. There was a high degree of consolidation of power in the hands of President Karadzic that existed throughout the war, Witness Milovanovic, transcript 16909. And this was argued in the Defence final brief at paragraphs 551 to 577 and 648. The Supreme Command, staffed with political leaders only, was the strategic decision-making body at the top of the VRS command, General Milovanovic, transcript page 16909. Remarkably, General Mladic did not have a right to vote on the decisions of the Supreme Command and was allowed to attend sessions by "invitation only," P3042. Other limitations on the general's authority include his inability to exert influence over the selection of corps commanders, which was the exclusive right of the civilian leadership, P2200. Nor could he influence the development of the six strategic objectives beyond normal military operations, Prosecution expert Donia, transcript page 15525 through 6; and General Milovanovic, T16973 through 4. Whilst the Prosecution has attempted to convince the Court that General Mladic and President Karadzic "talked about things as brothers" and that their aim was "to move together towards the same goal," transcript 44334, how is that view reconciled with the evidence of Karadzic's attempts to remove Mladic from his position as VRS commander, once in September 1993 and again 4 August 1995? This is discussed in the Defence brief, paragraph 565, and Prosecution Witness Skrbic at transcript 14012, 14013. Far from being a collective leadership working together to carry out the supposed common criminal plan, the relationship between Karadzic and Mladic did not extend beyond normal operational co-operation. This reveals no JCE could exist. This reveals reasonable doubt. The Prosecution argued in its closing arguments at transcript page 44332 that the Defence distorts the concept of chain of command and renders it meaningless. The Defence reiterates: General Mladic issued orders from the strategic level of command, but it was corps commanders at the operative level who decided how the action would be carried out, that's in paragraph 644 of the Defence brief and also in P2201, paragraph 2.5; and then the operative level corps commanders would decide how they are subordinates at the tactical level would carry out the mission. This is precisely how General Dannatt of the Prosecution described NATO armies as operating, P2629, paragraph 36. So why does the Prosecution have to disavow its own military experts time and again? The Prosecution wants the Chamber to believe that the accused wielded exclusive control over the VRS at all command levels, but this is not reflected by the evidence, Defence final brief paragraph 643 to 647. The accused was limited by the principles and structure of the VRS. He could not act with impunity, nor did he wield absolutely authority. Your Honours, I think we're again at the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I saw you looking at the clock already a minute ago, so I was confident that you would not forget it. We take a break and we resume at quarter past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have two corrections to the transcript that are the result of my mistakes. At temporary transcript page 21, line 20, what has been recorded as P3528 should, in fact, be P3258. And, again, that was because I misspoke the number. And also on temporary transcript page 40, line 15, I misspoke as to P2201, where I said paragraphs 4 through 9 and 11, I meant to say, paragraphs 4.9 through 4.11. And now I will resume. Lastly, the limited access to reliable communications and the inability to receive correct realtime combat-related information negatively affected the general's ability to effectively command and control subordinates. Whilst the VRS employed a comprehensive reporting system, including daily combat reports, these reports were compiled and given to the Supreme Command, and unless the general actively inquired about them, he was not made aware of them, Witness Trkulja, transcript page 35069 through 35072; Witness Banduka, transcript page 27310. There were instances where VRS subordinates would act outside their orders without the general's knowledge. This severely compromised his ability to effectively command and control the VRS forces. Prosecution Witness RM511 recalled serious problems with officers undertaking actions at their own will, transcript page 5068 to 9. In evidence we even have one incident that involved an officer who, without his commander's consent or knowledge, led a group with the intention of capturing Mojmilo. This group suffered serious losses and the Commanding Officer -- and pardon me, and the officer's move was described in evidence as reckless and not the behaviour of a properly trained soldier. And we have that in transcript page 5068 through 5069. The record also revealed why the accused had good reason to consider reports of internationals and international media unreliable. First, he considered the internationals biased against the Serbs. For example, I refer the Chamber to paragraphs 1728 to 1733 of the Defence final brief for UNPROFOR bias in Sarajevo, such as selective investigations and heavy reliance upon ABiH data and personnel, as evidenced by the testimony of several Prosecution and Defence witnesses such as Mole, Fraser, Thomas, and Moroz. Second, the accused was aware of all the disinformation spread by the ABiH, discussed at paragraphs 2507 through 2512 of the Defence final brief. These include BiH government and their frequent exaggerations of the situation to provoke an international response, D1298, paragraph 19. Third, we saw numerous examples of the international media misrepresenting incidents to the ABiH side's advantage discussed at paragraphs 2515 to 2517. In Srebrenica, UNPROFOR was well aware of weapon supplies to the ABiH through, for example, Tuzla airport, which was under UN control. It was a continuing effort to move weapons into Srebrenica and Zepa in order to keep the 28th Division supplied, expert of the Prosecution, Butler, at transcript page 16706 to 16707. For instance, a Turkish C-130 aircraft escorted by US F16s landed at Tuzla while the radars were turned off, D1240, paragraph 13. This aircraft supplied the Bosnian Muslims with weapon, Witness GRM037, transcript page 39017 through 8. However, no action was taken to prevent the Bosnian Muslim violation of the UN Security Council Resolutions prohibiting the import of weapons and military equipment. In contrast, force or actions against the VRS were just a question of "waiting for an event to occur." That was General Rupert Smith, transcript page 7417 through 7419. Although Srebrenica was meant to be a safe haven, UNPROFOR did not demilitarise Srebrenica in 1993 through 1995 following the demilitarization agreements. Similarly, DutchBat failed to disarm the 28th Division, P23, Witness Van Duijn, transcript page 10334 to 10336; Witness Franken, transcript page 10751 through 10752. Although the UN set up a weapons collection point in Srebrenica, Bosnian Muslims only surrendered old and non-functioning weaponry, D270, page 5; Prosecution expert Butler at 16793 of the transcript. And Egbers testified that these were weapons which were of no interest the Bosnian Muslim side, 13400 to 401. Again, no reaction of the UN. Smuggling goods through humanitarian convoys was also a common method used in Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde, D1615 and the testimony of GRM037 at 39018 of the transcript. Multiple UN officials even acknowledged that these convoys were used to supply the ABiH, transcript page 7528, General Smith; transcript page 10673 through 10674, General Nikolai as to Sarajevo. But they never took -- never undertook action to prevent it. Similarly, the UN was well aware of the black-market in Srebrenica, as Colonel Boering told us about at page 10038. If we can have the next slide. In addition, multiple witnesses have talked about UN bias and weapon smuggling occurred in Gorazde and Bihac. For example, in Gorazde GRM097 was shocked to see Bosnian Muslim soldiers descending from an UNMO vehicle, transcript page 40089, 40089. And as former UN officer Jan Segers testified, around Bihac even UN personnel were involved in smuggling for the ABiH side. Segers also stated that helicopters were being used to smuggle ammunition cases during the time of the embargo, D1465, page 4; D1466, page 3. A 29 May 1993 message from the Zagreb embassy of BiH - which we have up on our screen at the moment and in evidence that is D362 - confirms that extensive military weapons supplies were sent from Croatia to Bihac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm not sure that we have the right slide.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think we need the prior slide on that one. Whoops. Yeah. Now, General Mladic constantly complained about smuggling practices and the UN's role in this regard, D142, pages 1 through 2; P785, paragraph 57 evidence that. However, nothing was done with these legitimate complaints. Does all this evidence demonstrate that the UN was impartial and treating Serbs the same as the ABiH? No, it's open to another interpretation. Now if we can have the next slide. The record also revealed why the accused had good reason to consider the international media unreliable. At the time subordinates informed the accused that media reports were not objective; for example, at P3877, page 2, or that media reports were fabricated. And we have now on the screen P3951, page 3, which talks about. The Main Staff also believed that the media reports were unreliable. At page 45 of P338, the 1992 VRS combat-readiness report, we see "the orchestrated planting of lies about alleged massacres ..." and then we see "and other media fabrications served to project a distorted picture." BBC journalist Martin Bell substantiates the legitimacy of this belief held by the VRS when he testified at transcript page 7865 and 6 that international journalists employed the mind-set of the Muslims being the good guys and the Serbs the bad guys. At transcript page 7868, Bell noted that: "It was not so much a case of consciously taking sides as of not going anywhere outside the government-held parts of Sarajevo and seeing the war from that perspective." If we could have the next slide. This is significant because it is not enough for the Prosecution to simply prove that an accused received notice of crimes. I remind Your Honours of the Milutinovic case, IT -- pardon me, Volume 3 of that judgement, paragraphs 99 through 100. As in this case, in that case, President Milutinovic received reports from internationals and subordinates and the media, and the Chamber found that he was put on notice about crimes, that was at paragraph 270 of that judgement. However, this was deemed still insufficient at paragraph 276 of the judgement to satisfy the mental element for two reasons. First, the Chamber considered whether Milutinovic believed the information to be reliable and concluded that he did not. The Chamber stated that the information from the Serbian sources either made no mention of crimes or, when it did, the allegations were reported as propaganda by the international community. Second, Milutinovic believed that the relevant authorities were responding to the allegations. That's at paragraph 141 of Volume 3 of the Milutinovic Judgement. In the present case, although there were problems with the justice system, the accused reasonably expected the proper authorities would respond to offences. We saw that he delegated the responsibilities for initiating arrests and investigations to his subordinates, P3066; P244, paragraph 32; and the testimony of General Milovanovic at page 16953 through 4 of the transcript. And commanders were expected to be aware of their responsibilities in disciplining their troops. There was a procedure for serious criminal offences, P244, paragraph 33. Next slide. Furthermore, the accused himself repeatedly prohibited the commission of crimes, we have examples at P474, page 5, that's Directive number 1; D187; D1949; P1094; and P3673, page 6. And the Chamber has seen examples of subordinates reporting crimes up the chain of command and stating that they had or were responding to them. For instance, I refer the Chamber to P2843, page 2, that says: "An investigation is under way. A special report to follow." And P3818, which we now have before us that says: "Reprisals by soldiers on leave from the front ... but forceful action by the military police of the 1st KrK put an end to such behaviour." I note here that this report also makes clear that these crimes were neither ordered nor were they VRS policy. Thus, again we see reasonable doubt. Knowledge of crimes in itself is insufficient also because in many instances those crimes were committed by people over whom the accused had no authority. The Prosecution submits that Mladic "knew of crimes committed by Serb forces." And we saw last week, according to them, Serb forces includes civilian police, paramilitaries, and even local villagers. In such cases, as even Prosecution expert Theunens testified, the most that the VRS could do was to support such crimes to the organs in charge of those units; that was at transcript page 20624 through 5. And, in fact, we did see the accused repeatedly went to the relevant authorities. Taking paramilitaries as an example, we saw the accused's letters to President Karadzic at P3095 and D1503 as to Sanski Most.
