Finally, on the subject of knowledge, the evidence cited by the Prosecution should be carefully examined as they do not prove that the accused knew of VRS crimes. For example, it cannot be concluded from the accused being informed of deaths that he had reason to believe that those deaths were criminal and not unfortunate, but lawful collateral damage or lawful deaths of combatants. The accused having met with someone that he had a legitimate duty to meet with does not prove that that person informed the accused of an any crimes that he had just committed or was about to commit. Destruction of non-Serb civilian areas does not prove that crimes occurred when they could also have been legitimate military objectives. Evidence that a subordinate knew about a crime does not prove that the accused was actually informed. Reports of crimes that do not say who was responsible and in some places which clearly identify someone other than the VRS do not prove knowledge. For example, I refer the Chamber to P3951, where at page 3 it reports that the civilian police committed a massacre. Just as the general was not aware of the actions of his subordinates taken outside of the VRS chain of command, he was also not responsible for the criminal actions of outside organisations as they were separate from the VRS, for example, Crisis Staffs. If we could have the next slide. Crisis Staffs were not criminal organs. As Prosecution expert Witness Dorothea Hanson stated, they existed under Yugoslavian law, P379, paragraph 11 through 12; also Witness Milincic confirmed that at transcript page 28378 and we also see it from D732, paragraph 8. And Crisis Staffs were also used by the Muslims and Croats, P379, page 5, footnote 5. Crisis Staffs were intended to take over the lawful duties of running a municipality when the normal organs were unable to function during war time, D492, paragraph 5, for instance. The Chamber saw evidence of how they carried out regular governmental functions, such as maintaining utilities, obtaining food and supplies for residents, and ensuring running of schools, P413, page 6 through 8; D827, page 15, 87 through 88, and 91; P3913, page 6; P2414; P3172, paragraphs 2 and 7 through 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, can you just look at page 50, line 17, when you say page 15, 87 through 88, or did you say page 1587 through 88.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 15, and I probably did not pause enough, and then 87 through 88.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At paragraphs 447 through 460 of the Defence final trial brief, we see how Crisis Staffs showed concern for all citizens regardless of ethnicity. As part of their functions, Dr. Hanson acknowledged that Crisis Staffs were permitted by Yugoslavian law to undertake defence obligations, P379, paragraph 14. This included replenishing the war units which Hanson agreed was a pre-existing obligation and "not controversial," that was at transcript page 4206 through 4207. So military and Crisis Staff interaction is not criminal. The Prosecution has failed to establish a link between the Crisis Staffs and the accused. General Mladic had absolutely no role in their creation; he wasn't even there. From the beginning, Crisis Staffs were not to include military personnel as members, P408. At paragraphs 478 to 492 of the Defence brief, we review the evidence demonstrating that the VRS and Crisis Staff had completely separate chains of command. There we also discuss the existence of armed units created and commanded by Crisis Staffs and for whose conduct, therefore, the accused had no responsibility. The Prosecution concedes at paragraph 597 of their final brief: "No VRS witness testified that he had followed an order issued outside of his chain of command and no Crisis Staff member testified that he had issued an order to a VRS unit." At paragraphs 493 to 498 of the Defence brief, we also cite evidence proving that VRS members were not part of Crisis Staff decision-making, nor were they members, Witnesses Davidovic, Javoric, Basara, Adzic are just some of the evidence as to that. When VRS personnel were present at Crisis Staff meetings, their role was only to report on military matters and not to vote on the decisions. We heard from Colonel Basara at transcript page 34388. There were fundamental disagreements between the VRS and Crisis Staffs throughout the conflict, including repeated problems relating to Crisis Staffs' attempted interference with the armed forces. At one point, certain ARK authorities sought the removal of the accused as commander of the Main Staff, D839, page 5. These clashes are discussed at paragraphs 502 to 508. These clashes are evidence of reasonable doubt under the evidence and mandate acquittal. If we can go to the next slide. On the issue of disarmament in the municipalities, the evidence shows that contrary to the allegations, there was no criminal plan for Crisis Staffs to disarm non-Serbs so that the VRS could then attack the unarmed non-Serb civilians. First, in many cases, the VRS had not yet been formed when the take-overs were completed. Second, the Crisis Staffs, as municipal governments, were not only within their legal authority to disarm civilians but had a duty to maintain order. The instructions applied to all ethnicities. I refer the Court to D81, Conclusions of the ARK Crisis Staff, 18 May 1992, on your screens as we speak. Another separate organisation was the Serbian police force, the RS MUP. The RS MUP formed part of what is described as a broader criminal narrative in the Prosecution case surrounding the establishment of "parallel civilian and military structures" as a mechanism for ethnic cleansing rather than legitimate government. That's repeated at transcript page 44440 and in the Prosecution Pre-Trial Brief, paragraph 34. In reality, the RS MUP functioned as a vital public institution, ensuring order in the face of armed and aggressive Bosnian Muslim forces set on waging war against Bosnian Serbs. The RS MUP was a civilian organisation with an organised command structure answerable to civilian government structures. We have that discussed in our final brief at paragraphs 533 through 547. Any criminal act perpetrated by RS MUP officers was the responsibility of the minister of interior, who commanded the RS MUP units, and in that case that was Mr. Mico Stanisic. But the purported notebooks used by the Prosecution document Mladic's efforts to further law enforcement and compliance with the law. For example, in one of its citations the Prosecution uses to support Mladic's co-operation with Mico Stanisic at paragraph 511 of their brief, the following statements are found, and we're talking about P358: "To uncover the crimes and murders that occurred." And then also: "Who allows armed gangs from Serbia to come to the RS?" And that's at page 362. Another quote is: "The Law on Military Courts needs to be adopted." Page 363. And: "Investigate all abuses and punish them in the most efficient way." Page 365. Without the shroud of a joint criminal enterprise, these meetings are just the normal discussions between organs of a government system engaged in a conflict. The evidence lacks the ability to link the accused to the alleged crimes and is not the only reasonable interpretation. And thus, pursuant to paragraph 93 of the Gotovina appeals judgement, acquittal is appropriate. The Prosecution argues that the accused exercised de jure and de facto control over RS MUP, who were at times resubordinated to the VRS, this is at paragraph 530 of their final brief. Resubordination only occurred on an ad hoc basis; and even when resubordinated, the RS MUP remained within the rigid RS MUP chain of command, as attested to by the Prosecution's own insider witness, Momir Nikolic, who testified at transcript page 12093: "What I know for a fact is that they always had command and control over their own units when they would be carrying out joint tasks with the army." Colonel Kevac also provided that when joint operations were held: "They (VRS and RS MUP) operated as two distinct units, each carrying out their own assignments whilst helping the other to carry out their assignment. There is no suggestion that one unit had command authority over the other." That was at transcript page 30544 through 30545. The Prosecution's own evidence indicated that resubordinated MUP "shall be under the direct command of certain ministry officials," P3855. We heard evidence of co-ordinated action, or in B/C/S "sa dejstva," between RS MUP and VRS which is not resubordination. While the Prosecution would like you to believe that the RS MUP assisted in implementing the common criminal purpose by placing personnel at the VRS's disposal, the Prosecution then decides it doesn't even matter if the RS MUP are formally resubordinated or not; they still carried out criminal acts that fit within the definition of the common criminal purpose. We see that at paragraph 536 of their brief. This is reflective of the entire Prosecution argument. The link between the perpetrators of crimes and the accused, that's immaterial; the accused is guilty by virtue of his position and guilty because is he a Serb. If we can have the next slide. On the first day of closing arguments at transcript page 44387 through 44388, the Prosecution played an audio recording of an intercepted conversation, P403, between Gagovic, Unkovic, and Mladic, where Mladic is asked whether some of Arkan's Men were under VRS command. And Mladic replied: "All of them, all under arms are under my command, if they want to stay alive." P403, page 3, and we have that under the screen. Now, the Prosecution wants to you believe that this excerpt means that Arkan's paramilitary group were under Mladic's command, but the context of this excerpt does not support that conclusion. If we read further, we see that Mladic is recorded as saying: "So all should be under our command. No one should do anything on their own and a five-day truce must be observed." So the Defence offers a second reasonable interpretation of the meaning of Mladic's statement. Mladic sent various orders calling for the disarmament of paramilitaries, demanding that all paramilitary members place themselves under the command of the VRS if they had not committed any crimes. For those who had committed crimes, they were to be disarmed, arrested, and prosecuted in the VRS military courts, P501; and those unwilling to join the VRS should leave the territory. So this statement can be interpreted as Mladic meaning that any armed Serb should be a part of the VRS; and if they are not, then they would be pursued and removed from the area. The Prosecution has chosen one line and not presented this evidence in its entirety. We can move to the next slide. In further support of this interpretation, on 20 October 1995, the accused wrote a letter to Karadzic complaining about Arkan's men and criticised the civilian authorities' tolerance of him, this is D1503. Arkan's Tigers were subordinated to the RS MUP and Arkan was acting against the population and against the VRS. If we can go to the next slide. The Prosecution claims that the overarching JCE members "redeployed notorious volunteers and paramilitary groups such as Seselj's Men, the White Eagles, and Arkan's Tigers to BiH in 1992." And this is at paragraph 577 of their brief. Yet, Mladic's intent towards paramilitaries was clear: Paramilitaries were forbidden from operating in RS territory and criminal charges would be instigated against them if they chose to do so, again, P501. Despite the accused's attempts to incorporate former paramilitaries who were innocent men into the VRS, many of them refused. The standing orders of the VRS which prescribed that paramilitaries should be disarmed or integrated into the VRS remained unchanged throughout the war, Witness Corokalo, transcript page 28489. Mladic did not support nor approve of their actions, nor did he exercise command and control over them. Once paramilitary groups were incorporated into the VRS, they were no longer heard of. For example, Brne's Chetniks were split up with members being assigned to different brigade, so as to prohibit them from regrouping once incorporated. Colonel Radojcic testified about that at 23054 through 5 of the transcript. Their leader, Brne, was expelled from Bosnia. At paragraph 580 of its brief, the Prosecution attempts to imply that paramilitaries were incorporated into the VRS and were allowed to commit crimes on behalf of the VRS, thus making the link of the criminal activities carried out by the paramilitaries to the accused. The Prosecution also uses Mauzer's Panthers, a paramilitary group that was incorporated into the VRS, to try and prove their theory that Mladic used paramilitary to commit crimes in furtherance of the common criminal plan. The Prosecution claims that Mauzer's Panthers fought on the front lines, were eventually arrested for looting in July of 1992, and were never prosecuted and instead incorporated into the IBK. Mauzer's Panthers was an armed force set up by the Bijeljina municipality to defend the municipality, P3802, page 5; P1061, page 2. While it is true that the accused commended Mauzer in 1993, this was not a reward for his criminal behaviour. Witness Andan clarified that this commendation was awarded to unit, not to the person, T22410 through 22411 and P6579. Whilst it is also true that Mauzer and his unit were incorporated into the IBK, this was done at the local level, not by an order from Mladic. The Prosecution has not provided any evidence to show that Mladic condoned of any criminal actions. There were no orders from Mladic to Mauzer instructing him to commit crimes. A reasonable alternative explanation is that Mauzer's Panthers were incorporated into the VRS in an attempt to control and instill discipline over them. The allegation that Mladic used them as a tool in furtherance of the common criminal plan has not been established beyond a reasonable doubt. The Prosecution claimed that the paramilitary group called the Yellow Wasps were arrested, not charged with murder, despite a statement admitting to the killings recorded by the military police. The witness used to support this, Dragomir Andan, explains on cross-examination that 11 paramilitary members were charged for criminal activities and the others were deported because they could not obtain evidence to prove they had committed the crimes, transcript page 22425. While Mladic attempted to curb the criminal behaviour of paramilitary groups by incorporating them into the VRS and subjecting them to strict rules and regulations, he cannot be held accountable for those who refused to abide by these rules and acted out on their own. It is clear that these paramilitary groups acted for their own purposes and defied VRS command and control. Where possible, action was taken to prosecute them for their criminal acts. A main focus of the Prosecution is the allegation that the accused exerted influence over the military justice system to protect Serbs who had committed crimes, transcript page 44418 through 44419. We submit that at no time did the accused exert any kind of pressure on the military justice system. Indeed, the accused was personally supportive of the independent role of the military justice system, Witness RM513; D747, paragraph 8. The military judicial system was weakened by a number of factors which affected its ability to function. These included: A lack of resources, experts, absconded indictees, absent jurors, and staff shortages, P3560. It is important to remember that these courts were operating in challenging war-time conditions amidst the presence and prevalence of armed groups. The accused held a position of considerable authority in commanding the VRS, and there's no dispute that during that period crimes were committed. As the Defence has demonstrated convincingly throughout this trial and summarised in our brief, in most cases, responsibility for those crimes rests with those outside the VRS and in all cases with those acting outside of the accused's effective control. If we can have the next slide. Whilst the Prosecution was surprised that the Defence referred to the accused's 16th Assembly speech, transcript page 44371 through 2, believing it was evidence of the common purpose; the Defence argues otherwise. His speech, first as VRS Main Staff commander, was a call to act clearly and decisively, to be aware of the consequences of going to war and the importance of acting strategically. One of his first significant statements was at P431, page 35: "Therefore, we cannot cleanse nor can we have a sieve to sift so that only Serbs would stay or that the Serbs would fall through and the rest leave. Well, that is not -- that is -- will not, I do not know how Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic would explain this to the world. People, that would be genocide. We have to call upon any man who has bowed his forehead to the ground to embrace these areas and the territory of the state we plan to make. He too has his place with us and next to us." Critically, this statement was made following Karadzic's presentation of the six strategic objectives, effectively challenging the Assembly not to interpret them as calls for unlawful violence against Bosnian Muslims or Bosnian Croats. Mladic expressed a wish to galvanise all people born in the Republika Srpska and warned that any war should be waged only in self-defence. We see that in P431, page 33 through 35. By the way, this interpretation is supported by Prosecution military expert Ewan Brown at 19502 to 19503.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Ivetic, the Chamber would like to deliver a short decision. It is a decision on two Defence motions to admit a total of four statements pursuant to Rule 85(A) of the Rules. These motions were filed on the 5th and the 7th of December, 2016. The Prosecution responded to the motions on the 8th and the 9th of December, and the Defence filed a further response on the 9th of December which was, I think, formally distributed only this morning. The Defence submits that the four statement are crucial to a fair determination of the sentence, should the Chamber find the accused guilty. According to the Defence, the statements confirm the accused's good character. The Prosecution opposes the motions, arguing that the Defence makes no effort to show good cause for filing the motions more than three months after the deadline for such motions. It submits that the Defence fails to demonstrate that the interests of justice necessitate admitting the statements. With regard to three of the statements, the Prosecution submits that they focus on matters in controversy in this case, thereby falling outside the ambit of Rule 85(A)(vi) of the Rules. Should the Chamber admit the statements, the Prosecution tenders one document to provide further context. The Chamber recalls that it had set 25th of August, 2016, as the deadline for motions pursuant to Rule 85(A)(vi) of the Rules. The Defence requested an extension of this deadline, which was denied by the Chamber on the 2nd of September, 2016. A subsequent motion for certification to appeal the 2nd of September, 2016 a decision was denied by the Chamber on the 11th November 2016. The Defence has failed to demonstrate good cause for filing the motions at this stage, let alone acknowledge the just-mentioned procedural background. Nonetheless, the Chamber will consider whether it is consistent with the interests of justice to exceptionally deviate from the procedural requirements of admitting sentence-related information pursuant to Rule 85(A)(vi) of the Rules at this stage. The Chamber considers that the Defence had announced in August 2016 that it would like to tender certain sentence-related statements. The three statements tendered in the 5th of December motion contain information of direct interactions with the accused. The Chamber also considered the relationship between those providing the statement and the accused as well as the fact that the statements are very limited in scope. The Chamber further considers that the statements were tendered at such time early during the closing arguments, making it possible for both parties to still prepare and address them and make submissions on how they should be weighed. The Chamber lastly considers it of importance to give the Defence one final opportunity to have certain limited evidence introduced in this case. Under these circumstances, the Chamber find it is consistent with the interests of justice to exceptionally admit the three statements tendered in the 5th of December motion into evidence at this stage. The Chamber emphasises that this admission is limited to sentencing purposes. Any other information contained in the statements will be disregarded by the Chamber. The Chamber considers that the statement contained in the 7th of December motion reveals that a person giving the statement never even met with the accused. Further, the statement mainly deals with matters which the Chamber is unable to understand as being focussed on sentencing. Under these circumstances, the Chamber consider this statement to be of no assistance to the Chamber for sentencing purposes. In relation to the document tendered by the Prosecution, the Chamber observes that this document seeks to place in context certain information contained in the statements regarding whether Muslims were expelled. However, as the Chamber will merely admit the statements for sentencing purposes, there's no need to supplement the statements with further information in relation to certain crimes. Accordingly, the Chamber admits the three statements tendered in the 5th of December motion; denies admission of the document tendered by the Prosecution; and denies admission of the statement tendered in the 7th of December motion. Then, Mr. Lukic, the statements were submitted in a Confidential Annex. Are you tendering them under seal; and if so, what would be the basis for tendering them under seal?

utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Would you please reserve three D numbers for statements still to be uploaded by the Defence in relation to sentencing.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, those will be Exhibit D2182 through D2184.

utterances.text: Yes, and once they are uploaded and once we decided on them being under seal or not, we'll then further instruct you to attach statements to these provisionally reserved numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, provisionally, they remain under seal until we have decided otherwise. Then, Mr. Ivetic, if you're ready to proceed, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Also significant to the Prosecution's overarching JCE theory, the accused at this Assembly challenged Karadzic and Krajisnik, asking the rhetorical question that: If the six strategic objectives which they had just promulgated were interpreted genocide, that they would be unable to "explain that to the world," P431, page 35. The timing and context of this warning are critical to a proper understanding of the accused's state of mind. It is difficult to see where a commitment to the permanent removal of Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats could be inferred from a principled and robust, if understandably caution opposition to a more pernicious interpretation of the six strategic objectives and to the Bosnian Serb Assembly leadership. As argued in the Defence brief, if we could have the next slide, slid 13, that one. As argued in the Defence brief, paragraphs 795 to 796, the accused espoused principles of discipline and fairness, which are inconsistent with the intent of the overarching JCE. The accused commanded the VRS fully aware that ill discipline and criminality were counter-productive to military efficacy. General Mladic pursued peace and co-operated in agreements that called for a permanent cease-fire for the whole territory, D944, yet the Muslim leaders obstructed his attempts, with their forces performing offensive operations during the cessation of hostilities in Sarajevo. Mladic, in a letter to UNPROFOR Command, listed 803 violations of the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement between 23 December 1994 and 2 March 1995, that's D1665. The Prosecution use numerous statements made by others in Mladic's presence to prove Mladic's intent, but limited conclusions may be drawn about Mladic's intent from some selective inflammatory statements of politicians at meetings he attended. This is particularly true given the evidence that Mladic expressed his disagreement and at times made conciliatory statements at these meetings. The terms "Strategic Objectives" and "Strategic Goals" can have two different meetings. The six political Strategic Objectives or legitimate military operations which the Prosecution has not acknowledged, thus causing confusion when references to goals or objectives in military orders could be in reference to legitimate military targets or the political objectives. For example, at footnote 2125 of the Prosecution brief, the standing orders of the RS Assembly of 12 May 1992, when the objectives were adopted, refers to them as "Strategic Goals." Citation footnote 2352 of the Prosecution brief, a VRS order signed by the accused, refers to "achieving the Strategic Goals in 1994," P4268, page 6. Yet at citation military expert Theunens and the VRS combat report refers to them as "objectives," P3029 and P324. The distinction between the two terms is important, as the Prosecution - at the beginning of each municipality analysis and throughout its brief - attempt to link alleged crimes with the political Strategic Objectives. Kelecevic was asked about drawing this link with Directive 1 at transcript page 37378 and he replied: "No. One cannot formulate it that way. The goal was always to keep those who were loyal and who forwarded the policies of Republika Srpska and who were prepared to stay in the area, to keep them in the area, and include them in the armed force rather than separating the peoples in a very determined way." If we can have the next slide. The accused demonstrated his intent to prohibit the abuse of civilians by issuing orders to protect civilians from violence. These were not toothless or superficial, as the Prosecution wants you to believe, but examples that show reasonable doubt that the accused was the member of a JCE furthering a common criminal plan. P474 is what we see before us and we've talked about it already, and we see on this slide the protections ordered by General Mladic for civilians and for POWs. Next slide. D187, also issued by Ratko Mladic, and I read item number one: "The cruel treatments are severely forbidden as well as abuse and physical destruction of civil population, prisoners of war, and members of the international organisations." Next slide. D1514, we have an order from the accused dated 28 November 1992 that says: "According to available data, unknown persons disturbed Muslim population in S. Burati and Vrhbarje. In this regard: Order: I immediately take measures to protect Muslim population in these villages from possible violence from individuals, because they expressed loyalty to the Republika Srpska." Next slide. And the VRS did take --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I think there was a wrong quotation. It was not "I immediately," but "1 immediately." It was a numerical 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the VRS did take efforts to protect non-Serbs from violence. At D424, paragraph 3, we have the 1st KK command protecting the Muslim population from locals: "The actions of irresponsible individuals have caused uneasiness among the Muslim population in the villages of Batkovac and Stari Majdan ... The first KK command intervened by sending a military police platoon to protect the population from irresponsible individuals." But, as generally occurs in a war, there was considerable migration. There were a number of reasons for migration not attributable to Mladic or the VRS addressed at paragraphs 778 through 779 of the Defence brief. For example, there were concerns about safety and fear of the war spreading. If we could skip one slide and go to slide 19. There were several reasons why more non-Serbs would have left their homes. There were instructions from the Muslim and Croat authorities themselves. We have D699, paragraph 31; D884, paragraph 20, for example; and then we have here on the screen, D193. SDA instructions for moving out of Trebinje that state: "Through our activists stimulate all Muslims, especially prominent and wealthy ones, to leave Trebinje as soon as possible and cross over onto Montenegro. Do not shy away from using pressure or even force against Muslims who do not observe this order."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There were instances where civilians were temporarily removed from an area, as discussed at paragraphs 780 to 781 of the Defence brief. Under international humanitarian law, the displacement of civilian populations is permissible under two alternative grounds: "The security of the population or imperative military reasons so demand." I refer the Court to paragraph 93 of the Gotovina appeals decision, where that Chamber noted that certain evidence relied on to prove a JCE could have referred to: "A lawful consensus on helping civilians temporarily depart from an area of conflict for reasons, including legitimate military advantage and casualty reduction. Thus, discussion of pretext for artillery attacks of potential civil departures and of provision of exit corridors could be reasonably interpreted as referring to lawful combat operations and public relations efforts." The Prosecution asks the Chamber to consider all actions taken by the alleged JCE members as taken in pursuit of that common criminal purpose at paragraphs 499 to 528 of their brief. It fails to address alternative, equally available explanations reasonable under the evidence, especially that Mladic would be working with government officials in the furtherance of his lawful military duties. Numerous meetings between Mladic and civilian leaders would be completely lawful and expected. The 11 alleged members, with the exception of Arkan, were RS or Serbian government officials. The accused had a legal duty to meet and discuss the military situation with members of the RS Presidency. In attempting to use meetings notes and transcripts to prove co-operation, the Prosecution has actually highlighted the absence of any discussion of any criminal plan. Although there were various detention centres clearly established and run by different group, the Prosecution submits that they were actually one system. The truth fact is that VRS ran only two detention visits: Manjaca and Batkovic. Manjaca was first established in late 1991 by the JNA and then it was closed down and later re-opened as a POW camp to hold suspects accused of attacks on the military; it is discussed at paragraphs 510, 705 to 726, and 839 to 906 of the Defence brief. The Prosecution has argued that most prisoners at Manjaca were civilians and that there was no basis for their detention. However, the evidence demonstrated that there were -- that there was a detailed admission procedure for POWs and suspected combatants and all detainees were registered. P6993 reveals that investigations had taken place that substantiated the legitimacy of the detentions, for example, for illegally obtained weapons. Batkovic was established on 2 July 1992 as a POW facility by an IBK order, P3979. It held POWs and individuals suspected of committing criminal acts or war crimes. The order at P3906 says: "Prisoners for whom there are grounds for suspicion that they have committed criminal acts or crimes against humanity or war crimes shall be transferred and secured to the Batkovici prison camp." All POWs were registered by the Red Cross at Batkovic upon arrival. Batkovic is discussed at paragraphs 705 through 726 and 1628 through 1647 of the Defence brief. From the beginning, the accused repeatedly ordered subordinates to comply with international humanitarian law. All units of the VRS were ordered to treat POWs in accord with the Geneva Conventions. We already saw Directive 1 on that. P377 was a June 1992 Main Staff order including to the warden at Manjaca regarding proper treatment of POWs. The order establishing Batkovic, P3979 and P4448 which was incorrectly written as D448 in footnote 1500 of our brief, states that: "Organisation of work and care for prisoners in POW camp shall be carried out in accordance with the Geneva Conventions." The Prosecution describes dire conditions at Manjaca but hardship was felt throughout the region at that time. At P217, page 2, we see a 13 June 1992 1st Krajina Corps report confirming the scarcity. "The overall situation in the entire AOR is constantly deteriorating, especially in regard to the provision of supplies, to the region as a whole, and the struggle for food." At D847, paragraph 19, Bosko Amidzic corroborated the grim situation. The VRS did all it could in the circumstances. At paragraphs 714 to 716 of the Defence brief, we discuss that food given to detainees at Manjaca and Batkovic was the same as that given to guards and VRS soldiers. See, for example, transcript page 29470 and 471, Amidzic. A detainee described at P3134, pages 43 to 44: "We were better fed in Manjaca than the Chetniks that were securing us. We had three meals. We had a quarter of bread for every meal, and they asked food from us." In response to the shortages, VRS solicited the aid of outside charities, such as Merhamet and ICRC to improve conditions. RM051 testified about that and we see it in P2880. They would inspect the facilities and provide what was needed, such as equipment, cleaning material, and hygiene products. Witnesses RM051 and Amidzic testified as to that. During the initial stages of the centre, Merhamet visited Manjaca at least once or twice a week. Later, the ICRC typically visited the camp once a week; RM051 told us that. We heard descriptions of abuse and poor conditions at the facilities, but the relevant question is: How much did the accused know? At paragraph 24 and 31 of its Banja Luka summary, the Prosecution states that Mladic was aware of crimes and poor conditions in Manjaca in 1992 but the footnote contains only two documents. If we can have the next slide. One is P230, which is a report from Colonel Vukelic on the ICRC's visit. The colonel refers to ICRC observations about quantities of food and weight loss and says: "They had no valid points to corroborate their observations." Later on, the same document says: "Their dissatisfaction is not the result of conditions in the camp, but the former representative hinted that they were not acting in good faith." Based on this letter, Mladic reasonably would not have believed there was any abuse. Prosecution Expert Brown based his view that the Main Staff were aware of "what was happening inside Manjaca," on this letter at transcript page 19538. But as Brown conceded at transcript page 19544, Colonel Vukelic was actually providing reasons why the ICRC's criticisms were not justified, rather than reporting actually on the poor conditions. At P3805, we saw another report to Mladic, and again it report ulterior motives saying: "We declare with full responsibility that the purpose of his visit was not inspecting of the state of human rights but on the contrary, intelligence reconnaissance." This type of reporting up the chain of command was prevalent with subordinates reporting that internationals had ulterior motives and that media reports were inaccurate, for example, P2899 and P3877. Subordinates also reported that aid organisations were satisfied with conditions, for instance, P6993. The second document cited by the Prosecution to prove the accused's knowledge is P2880, the 7 August 1992 letter from Karadzic about the ICRC's recommendations. Next slide. If we follow what happened next, we see that five days later, at P2881, the accused wrote a letter to the warden marked "urgent" and listed several actions to be taken to improve conditions. And now I quote from the document that's before us: "The prisoners are to be secured, adequate accommodation, meals in the amount of 2800 calories per person per day, uninterrupted water supply. "All the prisoners who are wounded, sick or handicapped are to be transferred to a special facility ... "All manner of abuse, physical assaults, and beatings of the prisoners are to terminate immediately. "Take into consideration a possibility of releasing civilian prisoners." On Monday at transcript page 44404, the Prosecution described mistreatment at Batkovic from a witness who did not testify orally. However, there was no evidence that the accused was aware of the so-called special unit or any other alleged abuse. The Chamber heard from Colonel Todorovic, who confirmed that he was responsible for investigating allegations of crime or abuse at Batkovic. This was transcript page 19837 through 8. Todorovic testified that he at no point received information, officially or unofficially, of any human rights violations, and therefore he did not take steps to inform the Main Staff of any abuse. Transcript page 19838 to 19839. Before we go any further, we would like to stress that Mr. Tieger has acknowledged at transcript page 44376 that the Prosecution is no longer proceeding with its case in relation to Kalinovik, and we therefore seek an acquittal on those charges relating to Kalinovik.
